paragraphs: Recovering a person's body and movement from video requires aligning a model with the observed images. A-NeRF learns a generative body model from unlabeled, single-camera videos, extending neural radiance fields with a skeleton so that the representation can accommodate articulated motion over time.

The central technical issue is how spatial locations relate to moving body parts. Explicit surface models use forward kinematics to move a body with its skeleton; the implicit representation needs an inverse relationship. The paper introduces spatial latent variables relative to body-part poses, using an overparameterized representation to handle inverse operations that would otherwise be ill-posed.

This construction lets the method learn volumetric shape and appearance from scratch while jointly refining pose. The input videos require no ground-truth appearance, pose, or three-dimensional shape labels. Evaluations report improved accuracy on diverse datasets for rendering previously unseen viewpoints and capturing motion. The contribution connects image generation and pose refinement within a learned, articulated body representation.
neurips-2021-a-nerf-articulated-neural-r.tldr: A-NeRF learns an articulated body representation from unlabeled monocular video while jointly refining shape, appearance, and pose.

paragraphs: Scientific models often describe change through ordinary differential equations, but learning their unknown components from data can require repeatedly solving those equations. This paper addresses the resulting computational burden by bringing numerical solution and statistical inference into a shared probabilistic state-space formulation.

The approach builds on differential-equation solvers that express numerical solution as Bayesian filtering. That formulation makes it possible to incorporate latent force models directly into the equation and estimate the unknown force together with the evolving solution. An extended Kalman filter and smoother perform approximate Bayesian inference for both quantities in one pass with linear complexity, at a cost comparable to computing a single differential-equation solution.

The authors demonstrate the algorithm's expressiveness and performance through applications including a nonparametric SIRD model trained on COVID-19 outbreak data. The methodological contribution is the integration itself: treating the solver probabilistically allows information from observations and the governing equation to participate in the same inference procedure, reducing the need for repeated separate solves.
neurips-2021-a-probabilistic-state-space.tldr: A probabilistic state-space formulation jointly estimates differential-equation solutions and latent forces at roughly the cost of one numerical solve.

paragraphs: Scientific theories can predict patterns across many causal variables, making them difficult to express through a few conventional causal quantities. This paper introduces the Maximum Causal Set Effect, or MCSE, to turn these broader questions into an explicit statistical target that can be estimated and tested.

MCSE asks for the largest difference in causal effects associated with two sets of causal variables, with the probability of those sets occurring specified by the researcher. That probability requirement is part of how the query is defined. It gives the framework a way to express a broad causal comparison while retaining a concrete quantity for statistical analysis.

Under assumptions described as standard in causal inference, the proposed estimator is consistent as sample size grows and conservative in finite samples. It also has asymptotic normality and supports the nonparametric bootstrap, enabling classical inference. Comparisons with latent-variable approaches uncover larger causal effects in real and simulated data, demonstrating how the chosen formulation can reveal effects that those alternatives capture less strongly.
neurips-2021-answering-complex-causal-qu.tldr: MCSE formalizes broad causal questions as maximum effect differences between probability-constrained sets and provides an estimator with conditional statistical guarantees.

paragraphs: Generative flows and diffusion models have largely been applied to data with ordered values. This paper develops two ways to apply these model families to categorical observations, including text and image segmentation maps. The challenge is to construct a learning process that works directly with categories.

Argmax Flows combine a continuous probability distribution with an argmax operation that selects a category. Training requires connecting observed categories back to the continuous representation. The authors do this by learning a probabilistic inverse of argmax, allowing categorical observations to be lifted into continuous space for optimization.

Multinomial Diffusion follows a different route: a forward process gradually introduces categorical noise, and the model learns the corresponding generative denoising process. Both constructions adapt an established generative framework to categorical distributions through an explicit treatment of the data type. In text modeling and segmentation-map modeling, the paper reports better log-likelihood than existing dequantization approaches. These findings concern how well the models assign probability to the evaluated categorical data.
neurips-2021-argmax-flows-and-multinomia.tldr: Argmax Flows and Multinomial Diffusion adapt flow and diffusion models to categorical data, improving reported likelihood over dequantization approaches.

paragraphs: Learning navigation from visual demonstrations can work well in rich environments yet struggle when the environment changes. The paper attributes part of this difficulty to discrete-time neural models failing to account for causal relationships between an agent and its surroundings. It investigates continuous-time networks as a way to learn those relationships.

The authors develop both a theoretical and an experimental framework for causal representation learning with continuous-time neural networks. Their application is drone control from raw visual inputs, trained through imitation learning. The evaluated tasks span short- and long-term navigation as well as pursuing static and moving objects in photorealistic environments.

The reported results show robust navigation in tested settings where advanced recurrent models fail. They also demonstrate that the continuous-time models can learn complex causal control representations directly from visual observations and handle a variety of tasks. The significance is that the model's treatment of temporal dynamics becomes part of the approach to generalization, alongside learning which control actions follow from the observed scene.
neurips-2021-causal-navigation-by-contin.tldr: Continuous-time neural networks learn causal visual-control representations that support robust drone navigation across the paper's evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Imitation learning often assumes that demonstrations come from optimal experts. When demonstration quality varies, copying the available behavior can produce a poor policy. Confidence-Aware Imitation Learning, or CAIL, addresses this problem by jointly learning a policy and confidence scores that determine how demonstrations contribute to its training.

CAIL trains the policy using demonstrations reweighted by confidence. An outer loss tracks model performance and guides the learning of those confidence values. This creates a connection between the usefulness of demonstration data and the policy being learned, addressing limitations of earlier approaches that require manually assigned confidence or highly optimal demonstrations on average.

The paper provides convergence guarantees and evaluates the framework in simulated and real robot experiments. It reports significant improvements over other imitation-learning methods for demonstrations of varying quality. It further demonstrates successful policy learning without any optimal demonstrations, outperforming prior work in that setting. These results show that, in the evaluated cases, useful behavior can be recovered by learning how much to trust imperfect demonstrations.
neurips-2021-confidence-aware-imitation-.tldr: CAIL jointly learns demonstration confidence and a policy, enabling successful imitation from mixed-quality data even without optimal demonstrations in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Some statistical summaries belong to curved geometric spaces rather than unrestricted Euclidean space. This paper studies how to release such summaries with differential privacy while respecting their geometry. Its goal is to preserve useful statistical information when the valid outputs lie on a Riemannian manifold.

The proposed mechanism extends Laplace or K-norm privacy mechanisms using distances and volumes intrinsic to the manifold. The authors examine the Fréchet mean in detail, providing a central example of a statistical summary defined on such a space. Basing the mechanism on the manifold's own geometry makes the structure of the output space part of the privacy procedure.

The authors show that their mechanism is rate optimal and that its performance depends on the manifold's dimension rather than the dimension of an ambient space containing it. They also show that ignoring this structure can reduce the utility of the privatized summary. Examples cover symmetric positive definite matrices, relevant to covariance matrices, and spheres, which can represent discrete distributions.
neurips-2021-differential-privacy-over-r.tldr: A geometry-aware differential privacy mechanism achieves rate-optimal utility governed by a manifold's intrinsic dimension.

paragraphs: Privacy restrictions can make valuable datasets difficult to access directly. This paper develops DP-Sinkhorn, a generative method that learns from private data under differential privacy constraints. The intended use is to provide indirect access through generated data while imposing privacy protection during the learning process.

DP-Sinkhorn compares the model distribution with the data distribution using Sinkhorn divergence, a computationally efficient approximation to exact optimal transport distance. It minimizes this objective in a differentially private way and introduces a technique for controlling the bias and variance of gradient estimates. That trade-off matters because the gradient estimates drive how the generator learns.

The method avoids adversarial training objectives, which the abstract identifies as difficult to optimize, especially with privacy-induced noise. The authors describe the resulting approach as easy to train and deploy. Experiments report improvements over the state of the art on multiple image-modeling benchmarks and demonstrate private synthesis of informative RGB images. The findings support optimal transport as a practical objective for the evaluated private generation tasks.
neurips-2021-dont-generate-me-training-d.tldr: DP-Sinkhorn trains differentially private generators with an optimal transport objective and reports improved image-modeling results.

paragraphs: Understanding why a reinforcement-learning agent makes one move does not necessarily explain which moments matter to its final result. EDGE addresses this broader question by connecting complete game episodes to final rewards and assigning importance to time steps. Its explanations therefore concern an agent's strategy across an episode.

The method combines a Gaussian process with a customized kernel and an interpretable predictor. These components form a self-explainable model that both predicts final rewards and extracts time-step importance. To make parameter learning more efficient, the authors use inducing points and variational inference, supporting the learning procedure behind the explanation model.

Experiments on Atari and MuJoCo games assess explanation fidelity and demonstrate several uses of the resulting interpretations. These include understanding behavior, finding policy vulnerabilities, correcting policy errors, and defending against adversarial attacks. The contribution is a link between outcome prediction and episode-level interpretation: identifying influential moments provides a way to investigate behavior beyond the immediate choice of an individual action.
neurips-2021-edge-explaining-deep-reinfo.tldr: EDGE predicts episode rewards and identifies important time steps to explain reinforcement-learning strategies and investigate policy weaknesses.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search needs inexpensive ways to estimate how candidate networks will perform. One-shot estimators reduce training costs by sharing a supernet's parameters across candidates, while zero-shot estimators avoid training altogether. This paper asks how reliable these efficient estimates are, beyond their clear computational advantages.

The authors systematically assess both estimator families on five architecture-search benchmarks: NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-201, NAS-Bench-301, and the NDS ResNet and ResNeXt-A benchmarks. They use criteria tailored to architecture search to examine estimator behavior, including biases and variances. This makes the evaluation about the quality of information supplied to search, rather than efficiency alone.

For one-shot estimators, the analysis investigates why estimates are unsatisfactory and explores three perspectives for reducing the correlation gap. The paper then offers suggestions for applying and developing performance estimators. Its broader contribution is an assessment framework that future work can use to examine new estimators more comprehensively, helping distinguish computational savings from the reliability of the resulting architecture evaluations.
neurips-2021-evaluating-efficient-perfor.tldr: A systematic benchmark study examines the biases, variances, and reliability of one-shot and zero-shot neural architecture performance estimators.

paragraphs: Cooperative reinforcement learning requires agents to improve their behavior together. FACMAC tackles this in both discrete and continuous action spaces using deterministic policy gradients and a centralized critic. The critic evaluates joint behavior while being constructed from utilities associated with individual agents.

One construction combines those utilities through a nonlinear monotonic function, following the factorization idea used in QMIX. FACMAC also permits nonmonotonic factorization, expanding what the critic can represent. Empirically, this added capacity solves some tasks that the tested monolithic or monotonically factored critics cannot solve. A second design choice computes policy gradients over the entire joint action space, supporting coordinated policy changes across agents.

The authors evaluate FACMAC in multi-agent particle environments, a new multi-agent MuJoCo benchmark, and StarCraft II micromanagement tasks. It outperforms MADDPG and other baselines across all three evaluated domains. These results support the combination of structured joint-value estimation and coordinated policy updates, while the nonmonotonic experiments show that the form of the critic's factorization can materially affect success.
neurips-2021-facmac-factored-multi-agent.tldr: FACMAC combines a factored centralized critic with joint-action policy gradients to improve coordination in cooperative multi-agent learning.

paragraphs: The Sliced-Wasserstein distance compares distributions through an expectation over random projections. Its usual Monte Carlo approximation samples many such projections. This paper develops a deterministic alternative, using a property of high-dimensional probability to avoid the need to sample a collection of projection directions.

The key observation is that, under mild assumptions, one-dimensional projections of a high-dimensional random vector are approximately Gaussian. The authors use this concentration phenomenon to construct a simple approximation to the distance. The approach changes the computational strategy by exploiting the approximate form of projected distributions rather than estimating the projection expectation through repeated random sampling.

The paper derives nonasymptotic guarantees and proves that approximation error vanishes as dimension grows under a weak dependence condition on the data distribution. That condition is central to the high-dimensional guarantee. Synthetic experiments validate the theoretical findings, and a generative-modeling application illustrates the method's use. Together, these results explain when increasing dimension can help this approximation become more accurate.
neurips-2021-fast-approximation-of-the-s.tldr: A deterministic Sliced-Wasserstein approximation uses approximately Gaussian projections, with error vanishing in high dimensions under a weak dependence condition.

paragraphs: Nonlinear model predictive control repeatedly solves optimization problems as new sampling times arrive and the planning horizon advances. This paper studies a real-time iteration scheme for that setting, focusing on how to make the online optimization converge from arbitrary starting points under the stated generic assumptions.

The proposed change selects the step size of each Newton update using a differentiable exact augmented Lagrangian. Many existing real-time iteration schemes instead always take a full Newton step. The method also adapts the augmented Lagrangian's penalty parameters during operation, and the authors show that these parameters stabilize after certain periods.

The convergence result states that the subproblems' KKT residuals approach zero from any initial point, under the assumptions of the analysis. This specifies convergence in terms of optimality conditions rather than guaranteeing a globally optimal solution to every nonlinear problem. A central proof step establishes continued decrease of the augmented Lagrangian as the horizon moves forward. A numerical experiment demonstrates the claimed convergence behavior.
neurips-2021-global-convergence-of-onlin.tldr: Adaptive Newton step sizes yield global convergence of online MPC subproblem KKT residuals under the paper's assumptions.

paragraphs: Classical multidimensional scaling embeds data into Euclidean space from pairwise dissimilarities. This paper shows why adding embedding dimensions can sometimes make that representation worse. The authors derive a formula for the Frobenius error between the original dissimilarities and the distances produced by classical multidimensional scaling.

The formula depends on eigenvalues of a matrix derived from the input. When that matrix has a significant number of negative eigenvalues, error can initially decrease and then increase as dimensions are added. Experiments verify this behavior for several non-Euclidean metrics. On benchmark datasets, the resulting degradation also reduces classification accuracy for both nearest-neighbor and multilayer neural-network classifiers.

The analysis motivates an efficiently computed replacement matrix that is at least as close to the original distances as the closest Euclidean metric in the stated comparison. The replacement is itself not a metric. When used as input to classical multidimensional scaling, it empirically prevents distance error from increasing with dimension and reduces the degradation in classification accuracy.
neurips-2021-how-can-classical-multidime.tldr: Classical multidimensional scaling can worsen as dimensions increase, and a derived preprocessing method empirically reduces this degradation.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer an agent's reward function from its actions. The fundamental difficulty is ambiguity: even perfect knowledge of optimal behavior may be compatible with multiple rewards. This paper studies how that ambiguity can be resolved in problems with entropy regularization.

For a fixed environment, the authors fully characterize the reward functions that produce a given policy. They then show that observing behavior for the same reward under two distinct discount factors, or under sufficiently different environments, can identify the reward up to an additive constant. The requirement of a shared reward and the conditions on the observations are essential parts of this result.

The paper also establishes general necessary and sufficient conditions for reconstructing rewards that do not change with time over finite horizons, and for rewards independent of the chosen action. These results clarify what behavior can reveal about an underlying objective. Their contribution is a characterization of recoverability, identifying when additional behavioral settings provide enough information to resolve reward ambiguity.
neurips-2021-identifiability-in-inverse-.tldr: For entropy-regularized inverse reinforcement learning, the paper characterizes reward ambiguity and conditions that identify rewards up to a constant.

paragraphs: A fixed location in successive video frames may show different physical content because objects or the camera move. Treating time like another spatial dimension can therefore overlook the correspondences needed to understand motion. This paper develops trajectory attention to incorporate those correspondences into video transformers.

Trajectory attention is a drop-in block that combines information along implicitly determined motion paths. Its organizing principle is to gather information according to how scene content moves through the video. The authors additionally propose a method addressing the quadratic growth of attention computation and memory with input size, a concern that becomes especially important for long videos or high-resolution frames.

The paper evaluates these ideas through transformer-based video action recognition, reporting state-of-the-art results on Kinetics, Something-Something V2, and Epic-Kitchens. These findings support the approach in the tested recognition setting. The contribution combines a motion-aware way of collecting temporal information with a computational method intended to make larger video inputs more manageable.
neurips-2021-keeping-your-eye-on-the-bal.tldr: Trajectory attention aggregates video information along implicit motion paths and achieves reported state-of-the-art action recognition results.

paragraphs: Forecasting a chaotic system depends heavily on estimating its state accurately at the forecast's start. Data assimilation combines noisy, incomplete observations with a numerical dynamics model to obtain that estimate. This paper introduces amortized assimilation, a self-supervised framework that learns how to perform this combination.

The architecture joins neural denoising with differentiable simulation. Separate neural networks assimilate particular types of observation, while the simulator and shared recurrent memory connect the subtasks and their gradient flow. This lets the different observation-processing components participate in a shared learning process grounded in the system's dynamics.

The resulting training objective has an unbiased estimator of the true state as a minimizer even when the training observations are noisy. This is a property of the objective, rather than a claim that every trained network necessarily attains that estimator. Numerical experiments across several chaotic benchmark systems show improved effectiveness over widely used assimilation methods. The findings support learning state estimation through the interaction of observations, memory, and simulation.
neurips-2021-learning-to-assimilate-in-c.tldr: Amortized assimilation combines neural denoising, differentiable simulation, and recurrent memory to learn state estimation from noisy observations.

paragraphs: User-level differential privacy protects a person's entire contribution, which may contain multiple samples. This paper develops and analyzes algorithms under that stronger protection requirement. It asks how the statistical cost of privacy changes when each user supplies more observations or when more users participate.

For high-dimensional mean estimation, empirical risk minimization with smooth losses, stochastic convex optimization, and hypothesis classes with finite metric entropy, the privacy cost decreases at an O(1/√m) rate as samples per user increase. Increasing the number of users gives the faster O(1/n) rate. These findings distinguish two ways of collecting more data that have different effects on privacy cost.

The algorithms use new private mean-estimation techniques whose error scales with the distribution's concentration radius rather than its entire range. Lower bounds establish minimax optimality for mean estimation and stochastic convex optimization. Together, the results show how repeated observations from each person can improve learning while preserving protection for that person's full contribution, with optimality proved for the specified tasks.
neurips-2021-learning-with-user-level-pr.tldr: User-level private learning benefits from more samples per person, with privacy costs falling more quickly when the number of users increases.

paragraphs: A knowledge graph can contain several different hierarchies, each imposing its own partial ordering on entities. An embedding that captures only one global hierarchy cannot express all these orderings adequately. ConE addresses this by representing multiple hierarchical relations alongside relations that are not hierarchical.

The model embeds entities as cones in hyperbolic space and represents relations as transformations between cones. Cone-containment constraints in different subspaces encode different hierarchies. This gives each hierarchy a geometric structure within the shared representation, allowing the model to accommodate heterogeneous orderings instead of forcing them into a single global partial order.

Experiments report state-of-the-art performance for hierarchical reasoning and for completion of hierarchical knowledge graphs. The abstract gives Hits@1 results of 45.3% on WN18RR and 16.1% on DDB14, with 0.231 MRR on DDB14. It also reports an average 20% improvement over previous best hierarchical-reasoning results across three datasets. These findings support explicitly representing relation-specific ordering constraints for the evaluated reasoning and completion tasks.
neurips-2021-modeling-heterogeneous-hier.tldr: ConE uses relation-specific hyperbolic cone constraints to represent multiple hierarchies and improve knowledge graph reasoning and completion.

paragraphs: Different views of the same underlying information can have complicated dependencies. Multi-view representation learning seeks a shared representation that captures those relationships. This paper proposes choosing that representation by maximizing how much total correlation it explains, aiming to preserve shared information in a succinct latent description.

The authors formulate this goal variationally and introduce a tractable surrogate objective. That objective allows observations from different views to be fused and calibrated in representation space. From an information-theoretic perspective, the framework also encompasses existing multi-view generative models, connecting those approaches through a shared account of the dependencies their representations capture.

The method extends directly to partial multi-view learning, where observations can be missing without a regular pattern. This matters because the shared-representation objective can still be used when available views vary across observations. Evaluations on multi-view translation and classification report improvements over strong baselines. The findings support using explained total correlation as a practical learning objective for combining views and extracting information useful to downstream tasks.
neurips-2021-multi-view-representation-l.tldr: A total-correlation objective learns compact shared representations across views and extends to irregularly missing observations.

paragraphs: This paper provides finite-sample theoretical guarantees for bidirectional generative adversarial networks. It bounds estimation error by comparing the latent and data joint distributions using Dudley distance. With appropriately specified neural network architectures, the resulting bounds are nearly sharp, giving a quantitative account of the learning approach's accuracy.

A notable feature is that the analysis does not require the reference and data distributions to have equal dimensions or bounded support. Removing those assumptions broadens the settings covered by the guarantee. The authors also extend the results to Wasserstein bidirectional GANs, but that extension does require the target distribution to have bounded support.

The proofs introduce neural network constructions that map one empirical distribution to an arbitrary other empirical distribution, potentially in a space of different dimension. They also develop a decomposition of an integral probability metric for analyzing error. These tools explain how the guarantees are obtained and are presented as useful beyond BiGANs. The contribution is theoretical control of estimation error together with reusable methods for related learning problems.
neurips-2021-non-asymptotic-error-bounds.tldr: The paper derives nearly sharp finite-sample BiGAN error bounds without requiring equal distribution dimensions or bounded support for the main result.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning can learn visual features from unlabeled images, yet those features may depend on incidental object co-occurrences or backgrounds. Such contextual biases can hurt performance when scene relationships change. This paper makes contrastive learning object-aware so that its augmentations can address these sources of bias.

The first component, ContraCAM, uses a contrastively trained model to identify image regions that distinguish an image from other images. An iterative refinement procedure improves its ability to locate multiple objects and their full shapes. These inferred locations then guide two augmentations: object-aware random cropping to reduce contextual bias and background mixup to reduce background bias.

The framework therefore connects self-supervised localization with the way training views are constructed. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness particularly when training images contain multiple objects or evaluation images exhibit background and distribution shifts. Those results support the idea that choosing augmentations with object locations in mind can improve the learned representation's behavior when incidental scene correlations become less dependable.
neurips-2021-object-aware-contrastive-le.tldr: Self-supervised object localization guides cropping and background mixing to reduce contextual biases in contrastively learned scene representations.

paragraphs: A network's previous training can shape how easily it learns a later task. This paper shows that, with weight decay, connections in successive layers may become mutually frozen. Such configurations can restrict adaptation even though the network remains intended for further learning on new data.

The effect has two sides. It can make updates more invariant to nuisance factors, providing a useful bias for subsequent tasks. It can also obstruct learning when a new task requires substantially different features. The authors find that local sensitivity to input is correlated with adaptability, connecting this freezing behavior to a trade-off between invariance and plasticity.

A simple intervention resets the mutually frozen connections. Experiments show improved transfer learning across visual classification tasks, with state-of-the-art results on some datasets. The effectiveness of resetting depends on target dataset size and the difference between pretraining and target domains. The findings therefore motivate selectively restoring adaptability, while recognizing that the same inherited configuration can provide useful invariance in other transfer settings.
neurips-2021-on-plasticity-invariance-an.tldr: Weight decay can leave successive layers mutually frozen, and resetting those connections can improve transfer depending on dataset size and domain differences.

paragraphs: This paper examines reinforcement-learning attacks that alter the action signal selected by an agent. The authors call this action poisoning and study it in both white-box and black-box settings. Compared with the existing attack models discussed in the abstract, the adversary has more restricted capabilities, creating additional design challenges.

The proposed adaptive scheme, LCB-H, works in the black-box setting for a broad class of agents. The main guarantee applies to efficient agents whose dynamic regret grows sublinearly with the number of interaction steps. Under that condition, the attack can make the agent follow an attacker-selected policy very frequently while incurring only sublinear attack cost.

For the specific model-free algorithm UCB-H, the paper establishes a stronger cost result: logarithmic expenditure suffices to induce frequent agreement with the attacker's policy, even with black-box access. These are conditional theoretical findings about vulnerability through the action channel. They show why analyzing only attacks on rewards or environments leaves an additional mechanism of interference unaddressed.
neurips-2021-provably-efficient-black-bo.tldr: LCB-H can steer qualifying reinforcement-learning agents through black-box action poisoning with sublinear cost, and logarithmic cost for UCB-H.

paragraphs: Sequential decision-making requires balancing actions that currently look rewarding with actions that provide information. This paper defines a set of Bayesian optimistic policies and analyzes their regret. In stochastic multi-armed bandits, that set includes Thompson sampling, connecting a familiar method to a broader policy-selection framework.

Any algorithm producing policies in the optimistic set receives a Bayesian regret bound of Õ(√(AT)) for A actions over T rounds. The authors extend their analysis to bilinear saddle-point problems, including zero-sum matrix games and constrained bandits. In those settings, Thompson sampling can leave the optimistic set and incur linear regret on some instances.

Variational Bayesian Optimistic Sampling finds a policy within the set by solving a convex optimization problem. It works with arbitrary posteriors, without requiring log-concavity, unimodality, or smoothness. The variational formulation also supports adjusting exploration, adding regularization, incorporating constraints, and linear policy parameterization. The contribution is both a regret-based criterion for policy selection and an optimization procedure for satisfying it across the considered decision problems.
neurips-2021-variational-bayesian-optimi.tldr: VBOS selects Bayesian optimistic policies through convex optimization, extending regret guarantees to settings where Thompson sampling can fail.
